clue.text: Hat Liberal discarded in recess

indicators.note: Something discarded is thrown out and gone for good, so the letter it labels leaves the hat's name behind.

parts.note: The bowler is the hard round hat of City clerks and Charlie Chaplin.
L is the letter British ballot papers and crosswords use for Liberal.

explanation.surface: A hat a Liberal has thrown away, lying in an alcove.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recess' offers itself as a break in the working day, and the sense wanted is the architectural one — a shaded nook you can stand in.
explanation.definitionFit: A bower is a leafy alcove or arbour in a garden, which is a recess in the sense of a sheltered hollow.

clue.text: Dreadful pub documentation

parts.note: A bum deal or a bum note is a dreadful one.
The map symbol for a public house.

explanation.surface: The paperwork handed out by a truly dreadful pub.
explanation.walkthrough: PH marks a public house on an Ordnance Survey map, a convention British walkers know from the map key and crosswords borrow constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: Bumph is the useless printed matter that arrives in bulk — forms, leaflets, circulars — so 'documentation' is its polite name.

clue.text: Twist unsettling re: new prices for car accessory

parts.note: To wind is to twist, as a lane winds through hills.

indicators.note: To unsettle something is to knock it out of its settled arrangement, so these letters will not stay in the order given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters — the colon counts for nothing

explanation.surface: A memo headed 're: new prices' takes an unsettling twist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twist' sits at the front where a definition usually sits, and the colon does its best to make 're:' look like a memo heading rather than fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A windscreen wiper is the blade bolted to a car to sweep rain off the glass — a fitting rather than part of the machine.

clue.text: Border in order, though not at first

indicators.note: What is missing is specifically whatever stood at the front, so the word turns up without its opening letter.

parts.note: A ship in good order is in trim, and something tidy is trim.

explanation.surface: An edging that was eventually put in order, though not from the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Border in order' reads as one phrase about a tidy edge; the split falls after the first word, and everything following it is instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A rim is the border running round the edge of a wheel, a cup or a crater.

clue.text: Problems for wine-makers: six detectives probing links

parts.note: Six in Roman numerals.

indicators.note: A probe pushes into whatever it examines, so the piece doing the probing ends up inside the other.

parts.note: Links between people are ties.
The CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the plain-clothes detective branch of a British police force.

explanation.surface: Vineyard owners are in trouble as six detectives look into their connections.
explanation.walkthrough: Latin vitis is the grapevine and -cide is the killing suffix of pesticide and homicide, so the answer is a vine and its killer stuck together.
explanation.definitionFit: Viticides are vine-killers — the diseases and chemicals that destroy grapevines — which is precisely what troubles anyone making wine.

clue.text: Hedonist elevated endless desire, elevated attempt to seize gold, on reflection

indicators.note: Lifted up a down entry, letters read from the bottom of the grid upwards, so the word arrives back to front.
To seize something is to close your hands round it, which leaves what is seized in the middle.
A desire with no end is one letter shorter, losing the one it finishes on.
Seen in a mirror the two letters swap places, so the metal's symbol arrives the other way round.

parts.note: Desire is LOVE; with no end it is LOV, and it is then stood on its head.
The second 'elevated' is not an instruction at all, just the plain word for it.
An attempt at something is a try.
Gold is AU, the chemical symbol, arriving in mirror image.

explanation.surface: A pleasure-seeker, high on desire, makes a lofty grab for gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elevated' turns up twice and does two different jobs: once as the instruction to turn letters upwards, once as the word UP itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A voluptuary is someone given over to luxury and sensual pleasure, which is a hedonist under a grander name.

clue.text: Cast will turn up in Cats, so there!

indicators.note: Turning up a down entry sends the letters back the way they came, from the foot of the answer to its top.
The letters are already sitting inside the words that follow rather than waiting to be built from them.

parts.note: Four consecutive letters straddle the comma here; read up the entry they come out the other way round.

explanation.surface: Someone insists the company will show up in the musical Cats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cats' is italicised because it is the musical, so 'cast will turn up' reads as theatre gossip about the company arriving.
explanation.definitionFit: To cast a line or a net is to toss it, the same verb for throwing something with a flick of the wrist.

clue.text: One considering the Universe dispersing stoic's gloom

indicators.note: Gloom that disperses breaks up and drifts apart, and letters told to disperse scatter out of their order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters — the apostrophe counts for nothing

explanation.surface: Thinking about the universe drives away a stoic's gloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dispersing' sits between definition and fodder and could belong to either — a universe that disperses is a real thing to consider, which is the trap.
explanation.definitionFit: A cosmologist studies the origin and structure of the universe as a whole, so the phrase is the job description.

clue.text: Wait at a late point of the evening, being between turns on the floor?

indicators.note: Whatever is between two things has one of them on each side, so the floor work is needed twice, once either side.

parts.note: A turn on the floor is a dance, and the plural asks for two of them.
The word itself, taken at face value.

parts.words: a late point of the evening
parts.note: Ten o'clock is late in the evening, and the hour goes in as a word.

explanation.surface: Hanging about late in the evening, stuck between two spins round the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wait' is the servant's sense — waiting on someone, attending them — and not the standing-about that the rest of the sentence pretends it means.
explanation.definitionFit: To dance attendance on someone is to wait on them and run to their every want, which is 'wait' in its old transitive sense.

clue.text: Small place initially without facilities for skating? Not quite — touches here and there

indicators.note: initially means take the opening letter of each of the two words
not quite means the word stops one letter short of its end

parts.note: having no rinks, the places where people skate, is rinkless

explanation.surface: A small town lacking an ice rink, almost but not entirely.
explanation.walkthrough: S and P open 'Small place'; a place with no rinks would be RINKLESS, cut short to RINKLES.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprinkles are small scattered amounts, light touches dotted about here and there.

clue.text: Top celebrities enthralled by notes from some contemporary composers …

indicators.note: To be enthralled is to be held captive by something, so the celebrities are the ones shut inside.

parts.note: A minim is the half-note of written music, and the plural is what the clue asks for.
The A-list is where the biggest names sit.

explanation.surface: The biggest names are captivated by the notes some of today's composers are writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notes' has half a dozen crossword senses — banknotes, memos, the sol-fa syllables — and the one wanted is the written half-note of a score.
explanation.definitionFit: Minimalists are the composers — Glass, Reich, Adams — who build pieces from short repeating cells, so the school is defined by its members.

clue.text: … and not enthralled by countertenors

indicators.note: Held captive by the word that follows, the letters are already in order and only need picking out.

parts.note: Three consecutive letters towards the end of the singers' name.

explanation.surface: Countertenors are not captivated either.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries the sentence on from 9 across, and 'enthralled by' is reused for the same job in both clues.
explanation.definitionFit: Nor is the conjunction meaning 'and not', the negative partner of 'or' in neither/nor.

clue.text: It may dampen expectation about cooked pies

indicators.note: Something placed about another thing goes round the outside of it.

parts.note: Expectation of something good is hope.

indicators.note: Pies come out of the oven changed from what went in, so their letters do not keep their raw order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, four letters

explanation.surface: Baked pies fall short of the expectation built up around them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It may dampen' works as a definition only as a whole phrase: the answer is the thing that does the dampening, not the dampening itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A hosepipe is the garden tube that carries water under pressure, so whatever it is pointed at gets wet.

clue.text: Publicity group is taking care of pop singer and other divas

parts.note: PR is the public relations outfit that handles publicity.

indicators.note: Taking care of someone means keeping them inside your charge, which is where the singer's letters end up.

parts.note: The word itself, taken at face value.
The Queen of Pop, still the first name most people reach for.

explanation.surface: A publicity team is looking after a pop star and the other divas on the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop singer' belongs to the wordplay and 'other divas' to the definition, so the answer is everyone in the dressing room except the one actually named.
explanation.definitionFit: A prima donna is the leading female singer in an opera and, by extension, any temperamental star — which is what diva means too.

clue.text: Youngster pursuing work recalled making illegal booze

indicators.note: pursuing means following, so the youngster comes after
recalled means called back, so the work is read backwards

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a work
a teen is a youngster

explanation.surface: A teenager follows up on some work that has been called in again, and makes moonshine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recalled' turns OP into PO, followed by TEEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Poteen is Irish moonshine, a strong spirit traditionally distilled illicitly from potatoes or grain.

clue.text: With Charlie and I involved, excitedly develop European road transport?

indicators.note: involved means wrapped up inside, so the two letters go inside the rearranged word
excitedly means in an agitated way, so the letters of develop are jumbled

parts.note: its letters are rearranged
C is Charlie in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Charlie and I get excited about developing a European road vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that an old bicycle is a whimsical example of road transport.
explanation.definitionFit: A velocipede is an early bicycle; the question mark admits it is a quaint kind of road vehicle.

clue.text: Bondage TV series not entirely scrapped, receiving backing of the French

indicators.note: receiving means the rearranged letters take in the turned piece
scrapped suggests things broken up and reassembled differently
not entirely means the last letter of the word is cut off
backing means the French words are turned round to read the other way

parts.note: du is French for 'of the'

explanation.surface: A bondage-themed television show gets partly axed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not entirely' trims only the word series, before the rearranging; 'the French' is the French for 'of the', not a reference to France.
explanation.definitionFit: Servitude is the state of being a slave or under another's control, which is what bondage means.

clue.text: Deliver sermon: quick to dismiss God, capturing Church uncertainty

indicators.note: A captor keeps what it takes shut inside, so both short pieces are held in the middle.
Dismissing someone sends them away, so the letter standing for the deity leaves the word entirely.

parts.note: Quick means speedy.
D stands for the Latin Deus, the abbreviation behind Dei gratia on British coins.
CH is how Church is shortened on maps and signposts.
An if is a doubt — no ifs, no buts.

explanation.surface: A hasty preacher drops God from the service while the Church wrestles with doubt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quick to dismiss God' reads as one phrase about a hasty unbeliever, and the wordplay needs it broken in two before anything works.
explanation.definitionFit: To speechify is to hold forth at length and self-importantly, which is what delivering a sermon amounts to outside church.

clue.text: Sources in Oxford and Cambridge chat endlessly regarding eights

indicators.note: sources means the starting letters of each of the two university names
endlessly means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: chat means talk

explanation.surface: Students from the two old universities gossip without end about rowing eights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eights' suggests the Oxford and Cambridge rowing crews, but the definition means the number eight.
explanation.definitionFit: Octal describes a number system in base 8, so it relates to eights.

clue.text: Blokes in A&E returned for medical intervention

indicators.note: An across answer that returns runs back the way it came, right to left along the row.
Blokes in a place are inside it, so their letters sit within the other piece.

parts.note: A&E is the accident and emergency department of a British hospital, and the ampersand is not a letter.
Blokes are men.

explanation.surface: The men are back down at casualty again.
explanation.walkthrough: A&E is what Britain calls the casualty department, so the surface reads as a night shift and gives away nothing about the treatment.
explanation.definitionFit: An enema is fluid introduced into the bowel to clear it, a procedure carried out on a patient — hence a medical intervention.

clue.text: Aussie creatures surrounding excavations? Lots of space

indicators.note: What surrounds a thing closes round it on both sides, leaving the diggings in the middle.

parts.note: Roos is the Australian short form of kangaroos.
Excavations dug for coal or gold are mines.

explanation.surface: Kangaroos standing round a set of diggings in the outback.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the picture is about space at all — it is pure outback, and the definition is the three words tacked on at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Roominess is the quality of having plenty of room, so 'lots of space' is the same noun idea in plainer words.

clue.text: Rancher wary, suppressing expression of pain in front of buckaroo, initially

indicators.note: To suppress a cry is to hold it down inside you, which buries those letters in the middle.

parts.note: Someone wary of attention is coy.

indicators.note: One piece stands ahead of the other, which settles the order the two go in.

parts.note: Ow is the noise you make when something hurts.

indicators.note: Only the letter the word begins with is wanted.

parts.note: The opening letter of buckaroo.

explanation.surface: A cautious rancher swallows a yelp of pain in front of a young bronco-rider.
explanation.walkthrough: A buckaroo is a cowpuncher himself, so the surface's rider and the definition are the same man — and the word is there for one letter only.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowboy is the hand who works cattle on a ranch, which is what 'rancher' names in loose everyday use.

clue.text: Yard probing juicy gossip over Government scoundrel

indicators.note: A probe pushes into what it is examining, so these letters go inside the phrase the others build.

parts.note: Dirt is the scandal people dig up on each other.
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over.
G is the standard abbreviation for Government.
Yd is the written abbreviation for the imperial yard.

explanation.surface: Scotland Yard digs into juicy rumours about the Government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yard' means Scotland Yard in the surface and the imperial measure in the wordplay, and the insertion lands exactly on the join between the answer's two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirty dog is a contemptible, underhand person — the old-fashioned phrase you would use of a scoundrel or a cad.

clue.text: Chap clutching stone, feeling effects of gale

indicators.note: To clutch something is to grip it in your fist, closing right round it.

parts.note: A chap is a guy.
St is the abbreviation for the stone, the British fourteen-pound unit used for body weight.

explanation.surface: A man hangs on to a rock while the wind does its worst.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feeling effects of gale' is a whole-phrase definition — no single word in it is a synonym, which is why it reads as more of the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Gusty weather arrives in sudden hard blasts, so anywhere feeling the effects of a gale is gusty.

clue.text: Case ends in outcome against you and I

indicators.note: The end of each word is where its letter comes from, taken in the order the words appear.

parts.note: The last letter of the word.
The last letter of the word.
The last letters of the two pronouns; a one-letter word is its own ending.

explanation.surface: The outcome of a lawsuit has gone against the two of us.
explanation.walkthrough: An etui is a small stitched box for needles and scissors, a Victorian lady's accessory that survives almost entirely inside crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: An etui is a small ornamental case for needles, scissors and other little tools, so 'Case' is its plain sense.

clue.text: Independent politician, a source of funny business?

parts.note: I is how Independent is marked against a candidate's name.
An MP is a Member of Parliament.

explanation.surface: An MP who sits for no party turns out to be behind some mischief.
explanation.walkthrough: The Independent is the paper the puzzle appears in and an independent MP sits for no party, so both readings are live and only one letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: An imp is a small mischievous demon, so it is a source of funny business in the sense of pranks rather than fraud.

clue.text: Country swamping the river in neon lights

indicators.note: To swamp something is to flood right over it, leaving it submerged in the middle.

parts.note: Ne is the chemical symbol for neon.
A bird lights on a branch when it lands.
The word 'the' followed by R, the map-maker's abbreviation for river.

explanation.surface: A country drowning its river under neon signs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lights' is a verb here, not a noun — a bird lights on a branch — and the phrase 'neon lights' is what the whole misdirection hangs on.
explanation.definitionFit: The Netherlands is the low-lying country on the North Sea coast, which many people know instead by the name of two of its provinces, Holland.

clue.text: Water movement lacking force, lacking strength

indicators.note: A word that lacks something has it taken out, and what goes is the single letter physics uses for force.

parts.note: Water on the move is a flow.
F is the physicist's symbol for force, and it is the letter that goes.

explanation.surface: A current with no push behind it and no strength left in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lacking' does two different jobs in one short sentence: an instruction the first time, part of the definition the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone low is weak or run down — low on energy, feeling low — rather than short in height.

clue.text: Factory at first trimmed wages after year in part of Northern England

indicators.note: What follows something goes behind it, so the year is at the head of the assembly.

parts.note: Y is the standard abbreviation for year.

indicators.note: Trimmed at its front, the word loses the letter it begins with.

parts.note: A factory is a works, as in the steelworks up the road.
Hire is payment for labour, the sense alive in 'the labourer is worthy of his hire'.

explanation.surface: A factory has cut its wages after a year, somewhere up north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' looks like a time word carried over from the surface's bad year, and it is really the pointer to which end of the factory gets trimmed.
explanation.definitionFit: Yorkshire is the largest of the historic counties of northern England, so it is one part of that region rather than the whole of it.

clue.text: Went quietly, finally exhibiting little strength

parts.note: To wee is British nursery language for urinating, and 'went' is that verb in the past tense.

indicators.note: The letter wanted is the one the word finishes on, and nothing before it.

parts.note: The closing letter of quietly.

explanation.surface: Someone slipped away quietly at the end, showing no great strength of will.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went' is the nursery euphemism — went to the loo — which is a long way from the quiet departure the surface offers.
explanation.definitionFit: A weedy person is thin and feeble, like a plant grown spindly in the shade, so they exhibit little strength.
